utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I understand, Ms. Gopalan, you have a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, just a short procedural matter, Your Honours. I would like to use the witness's statement from 1999 during the course of his testimony today. This statement was provided to the Defence -- they were notified of our intention to use the statement in the witness notification. We drew attention to the statement specifically, and the reason I'm requested leave at this stage is because we did not include the statement in our filing of 14th of January, 2009. The witness was led live in Milutinovic, and we only sought leave to use his transcript from the Milutinovic case. However, I think at this stage it would be beneficial and expeditious to use a concise statement, and that is why I'm seeking Your Honours' leave to use it with the witness and tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why was it not done with the motion which dealt with the transcript of the witness's evidence in the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you mean the motion where we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. There's been an extensive --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- that's true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That is true, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And in respect of this witness you put forward the transcript but not the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why is the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That is because the witness was led live in Milutinovic and therefore the statement was in use by the Prosecution then. Now, having reviewed the statement, I think it will greatly speed up the process because it's a concise statement. So it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll see what it is that the Defence feels about the matter. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given that we were notified late, in principle I'm going to object to it and this is all I have to say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: May I just add something, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan, we haven't called on you again, although I see you thought we might. The Chamber has noticed a tendency, not only orally but in -- also in respect of written submissions, for a motion to be moved with reasons, a response, and then further reasons which are really matters which should have been dealt with in the first instance, so we will not call upon you in response. On this occasion, we have had notice and has the Defence of the full oral evidence given in a previous trial of the witness. Defence counsel objecting in principle to what you move has not, though, identified any particular difficulty or difference that can be seen from what is now proposed to be added as, from your description, a short version, as it were, of what is in transcript evidence. The Chamber frankly is in two minds but has decided in the end that on this occasion it will allow the use of the short statement, but it is of two minds because the structure of the procedure is one which is designed to enable the Defence or the other party and the Chamber to have prior notice to be able to give consideration to a statement or transcript before the witness comes in court so that there can be attention given to any matter which on prior study has been identified. And to simply allow a witness to come and then tender without warning a statement is therefore likely to be disruptive of orderly preparation and could lead to some unfortunate issues. So with those words, please understand this is no precedent for what the Chamber will do should this sort of application be moved at some other time with some other witness. On this occasion, yes, you have your motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, we're most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kickert. Please could you state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: My name is Jan Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I'm Austrian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is your professional, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I'm a diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just a reminder, as we are both speaking the same language, and as you know there are translations and transcriptions in process, if we could just pause between question and answer. Thank you very much. Mr. Kickert, where are you currently posted?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I'm currently at Vienna at the foreign ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In June 1999, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to recently review the statement?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I re-read it again, yes, before coming here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the information contained in this statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 5240, and I seek Your Honours' leave to tender the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00478, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, have you previously testified in this Tribunal in the case of Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al in March 2007?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to recently review this testimony?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I did too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You had indicated that you wished to make some corrections to this testimony?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Just two minor corrections in -- on names. I just found out that at one page it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, Mr. Kickert. We can just get to that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If I could call up 65 ter 5214, and if -- yes. And could we go to page 5 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to see the page on the screen, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly the right page where Emyr Jones-Perry and it is not Mr. Fischer but Mr. Ischinger, so I must have -- and later on in the text it correctly states Mr. Ischinger; he was the political director in the foreign, German foreign ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And those are the names referred to in lines 9 and 10 of that page?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you also wished to make another correction and that was at page 64 of the same document. We'll wait for it to be called up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we have page 64 on the e-court, please. Thank you. And if we could scroll down the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What was the correction you wished to make here, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Again on the name. It's Bardhyl Mahmuti, Bardhyl is his first name: B-a-r-d-h-y-l.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And having made these changes, are you satisfied that if you were asked the same questions that you were asked in the case of Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al, that you would provide the same answers today?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I would like to tender the witness's testimony into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P00479, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, during the course of the witness's testimony I will be referring to a number of documents. I would like to hand over hard copies of these documents to the witness to ease the process of referring to these documents. They are in his original German language, which I believe will assist him in providing clearer answers to us in relation to the questions I seek to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will also come up on the screen for the Defence and the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, would you also like a copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd now like to read the summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: The witness is a diplomat for the Austrian government and was a second secretary in the Austrian embassy in Belgrade. In March 1998 the witness was part of a diplomatic corps which was taken to Kosovo by the Yugoslav Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The witness made several other trips in Kosovo. He describes the use of excessive force by the Serb forces during the 1998 summer offensive. In late July/early August 1998, a pattern emerged when the witness went on field trips. He passed villages going out into the field which were intact, and when he returned on the same route later these villages were destroyed or burning. He concluded that this destruction or burning was done by the police as they were the only ones he saw in these areas. He also saw many internally displaced persons and observed an increasing level of destruction of Kosovo Albanian villages which he also noticed were no longer inhabited. That's the end of the in-court summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, just a correction, the trip was in June 1998 taken to Kosovo by the Yugoslav Ministry of Foreign Affairs. There was a trip in March which I did not participate in, but in June I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kickert. Mr. Kickert, in your capacity as a diplomat, did you serve in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I was a diplomat posted as second secretary as you said to the Austrian embassy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: November 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Who was the mission chief at the embassy there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Wolfgang Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And while you were in the embassy, did you go on trips to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I started to go to Kosovo the first time in January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, in your statement, this is at page 2, paragraph 4, you refer to an outing to the -- to Pec and Decani in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would like to call up 65 ter number 2666.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Does this relate to the trip that you made to Pec and Decani in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report of the trip I participated in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who prepared this report?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to page 2 of this report that you prepared. At page 2 in the paragraph headed "Decani," you say or the report states: "Considerable devastation, but by no means as drastic ..." And you go on to say that the town appeared dead. Could you explain what you meant by the town appearing dead?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: In German I say "ausgestorben," that means that -- dead in the sense that no people were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I see. And you also say that the people you saw, the patrons on the main square, looked as though they were on show. What do you mean by the phrase "on show"?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, we were taken down to the area by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, on the invitation of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and to show us how they saw the situation in the area and also to show that they were in control of situation. And we had the feeling or I had the feeling - that's what I wrote in the report - that these few people, this was at the cafe at the crossroads in Decani where you go to the monastery, that there were just a few people apart from the police and that they were just placed there because we got off the bus so that we could see some people, else it was empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the next line you refer to the village of Prilep or in the next line below the paragraph on Decani, and you say "similarly extensive destruction." Could you describe this destruction?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: As I write in the paragraph on Decani, you would see impacts from bullets at the same time more obvious was destruction through fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what about the inhabitants in Prilep, did you see anyone there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I can't recall seeing anybody there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page of this document you refer to a briefing by the Yugoslav foreign minister and Ministry of the Interior. Do you recall who attended this briefing as a representative of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to another document now, Mr. Kickert --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Before I move on, may I tender 02666 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00480, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 2665, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, this is another report from the Austrian embassy, and it's dated the 1st of July, 1998. It's numbered 2665. Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the author of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in the summary section, in the middle of the page, the first tab says: "Official confirmation for the first time of participation of army units in inland operations." Had you had any information before on army units participating in inland operations?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, it was denied that the army was involved, that it was only a police affair, and this is the first time - and I cite Reuters, being told by Mr. Veljko Odalovic, that the Yugoslav army had participated in an action in Belacevac which is near Obilic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00481, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, in your statement you refer to a trip that was taken by Ambassador Petritsch and yourself. It was an inaugural trip for KDOM's arrival. This is at the top of page 3 of your statement. Can you explain what KDOM was?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: KDOM stands for Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, and the whole idea behind it was that we, as representatives of the international community, had difficulties to get accurate information. We would get allegations from one side and allegations from the other side, and so we wanted to have -- to make our own picture, that's why we wanted to have international monitors in Kosovo. And we have the European Union at that time, it was not yet the EU, but we had the ECMM, European Community Monitoring Mission, and we had to deploy one mobile team from the end of May there; and the Americans also wanted to be present, and there was some talks with Belgrade on officially allowing monitors from the international community there in larger number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you mentioned that the Contact Group ambassadors also came on this trip. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The Contact Group is -- the Contact Group on the Balkans is a group of the -- of six major powers, that is, the US, Russia, the UK, France, Italy, who have I left out, Germany, four Europeans, the Russians and the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Could I call up 65 ter 2664, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, this is another document from the Austrian embassy and is dated the 6th of July, 1998. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how does this relate to the KDOM trip that we just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: From the 1st of July, 1998, Austria was chairing the European Union, and for that purpose we are co-opted for this half year into the Contact Group as the EU Presidency and one of the tasks of EU Presidency is also to inform all other EU members on events. So what I've done is to write my report direct in English so that my colleagues in Vienna could transform this into what we call Coreu, meaning a correspondence, EU correspondence, that they could inform the other EU partners about this trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would like to tender 02664 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00482, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers make breaks between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We will.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In your statement you refer to various trips that you made to Malisevo in the summer of 1998. I'd like to focus on the trip you made with the EU troika, and this is set out in your statement in page 3. Could you tell us about this trip, please.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The Austrians -- we were the EU Presidency, and at that time you had the troika, that's the outgoing and the incoming EU presidencies, that's the troika; and this was a trip undertaken by Secretary-General of the Austrian Foreign Minister Rohan and the two political directors Wolfgang Ischinger from Germany and Emyr Jones-Perry from the UK.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What did you see during this trip?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: First -- the first part of the visit in Kosovo was in Pristina, talking to politicians, and then the decision was made that we would also go inland into Kosovo. And I remember that we were stopped by a police check-point at one stage, eventually let through, and went more inland and came back the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did you see anything during this trip when you went inland?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, the most remarkable for me was when we went inland we would see unharvested fields, and when we returned these fields were burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And do you know who was responsible for the burning?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody setting them on fire, but I didn't see any people but policemen around.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you have a specific area in mind when you say you went inland during this trip that you made?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: At this time most of my trips, because that was a time when we established contact with KLA, was to Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And did Malisevo have any special significance as an area?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, it was strategically located at a crossroads. It's a juncture city, if you like, north, south, east, west, and at that time when I went there it was what the KLA had called their capital.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And during the summer period, since you made a number of trips to Malisevo, did you recognise any changes to the city or were there any changes to the area of Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, at the beginning when I first went to Malisevo, it was controlled by the KLA; and when the KLA abandoned Malisevo, it was empty, hardly any people there; and it was then re-taken by Serbian security forces, by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And apart from your own observations about Malisevo that you made during your trips there, did you receive any other information from other sources about the situation in Malisevo during this period?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. By that time we had already established quite a good group of EU monitors, ECMM, and we received daily reports, weekly reports, because my -- as a diplomat my main -- primary occupation was not to make field trips but to leave that to the monitors. So we got from them very concrete reports of what they have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did you receive any specific information on perpetrators of anything being -- of perpetrators who participated in actions in Malisevo or that area?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. We received a special report on Malisevo where it -- our monitors reported that -- of destruction going on in Malisevo, and particularly two sentences where, one, they saw policemen looting the shops in Malisevo; and a second one was that they saw a policeman in uniform setting fire to a house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And roughly what time-frame would this have been?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That must have been the end of July -- end of July, maybe the first days of August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to a different topic. In your statement you refer to a number of trips that you made to Orahovac in the summer of 1998. Could you explain why you made these trips to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Orahovac is an ethnically mixed city, and there were some fightings in July; and the purpose of our -- of my visits was to try to establish a mechanism for people, IDPs, to return to the city, Kosovo Albanian IDPs to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter 2655, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if we could have a look at the first page, Mr. Kickert. This is a Telefax dated the 4th of August. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us why this document was prepared?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was a fax to my colleagues from the Contact Group embassies, US, French, German, Italian, and British, and it was about speaking points for a demarche, sort of an intervention if you like, with the FRY authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Can I take you to page 2 of that document and under the heading "major concerns" in the second bullet point you say: "Reports about looting and burning of houses and setting fire to unharvested fields by members of the FRY security forces." What was the source of this information, Mr. Kickert, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, that was the ECMM reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. And in the bullet point below you refer to the number of IDPs growing every day and the situation worsening. Are you able to provide an estimate of the number of IDPs, if you recall, again?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. I mean, we -- this point would have been based on report from UNHCR, ICRC, and the bigger international NGOs working in the area which I had contact with, that's Medecins Sans Frontieres, Oxfam.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the middle of the page under the heading: "Therefore we urge the FRY government to ..." The second bullet point you say: "Stop FRY forces damaging houses and property; prevent looting ..." Could you explain what sort of damage you are referring to here?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This bullet point relates to the second bullet points under major concerns. This is just telling them: Since we have reports, we asked them to stop these actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 2655 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00483, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, I'd now like to turn to the trips you made with Ambassador Parak. This is referred to in paragraph 3, page 4, of your statement and these trips were made, according to your statement, in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we call up 65 ter 564, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: It's a report dated the 11th of September, 1998. Did you prepare this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the author of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about this document, but firstly: How does this relate to the trip that you made with Ambassador Parak in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Parak was the head of ECMM based in Sarajevo, that was the headquarters of ECMM for the whole of ex-Yugoslavia, and he was coming down to Kosovo, and I accompanied him on a trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we have a look at this document, in the first bullet point you say: "Villages along the main Pristina-Pec road ... with the exception of Serbian villages, no longer inhabited." How could you tell that these villages were not Albanian villages?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: You could judge by way houses or compounds were built, whether there was a mosque or an Orthodox church, and this particular one was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did you see anyone in this village?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I recall in this particular village that I saw a civilian walking around with a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we go a few bullet points down, the paragraph beginning: "Junik has been little damaged ..." There you say: " ... there is nothing to be seen of the 1.000 people who have returned home from the Serbian side ..."

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, that's an incorrect translation. What I've written in German is that there's nothing to be seen of the thousand persons the Serb side claimed that have -- to have returned. The Serb side claimed a thousand persons have returned, but when we went in there, we didn't see enough people to substantiate that this claim was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could you explain a little bit the background that led to this claim being made?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, the whole situation in summer, since end of July there was clearly an offensive going on by the Serbian security forces against the KLA, and because of this fighting there were huge numbers of IDPs; and the big concern of the international community is: Could we create circumstances that these IDPs would return. So whenever there were claims of pockets of IDPs, UNHCR would try to contact them and we would, through our monitors mainly, would check whether reports of these pockets or of returnees are accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, you mentioned IDPs, and at the top of page 2 of this document there is a reference to 25.000 internally displaced persons. Do you recall what the source of this figure was?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We would not rely on IDP figures from either the Kosovo Albanian or the Serbian side. Most likely is this number from UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the bullet point below you refer to forced transportation of internally displaced persons to Pec. Could you explain, please, what you meant by "forced transportation."

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's the ECMM -- I cite that the ECMM reported that people were taken -- taken from the area where they were located to Pec; and since Pec was controlled by the Serbian security forces, it can only be that the Serb -- Serbian authorities have taken them to Pec.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And finally in the summer section of this document the first bullet point you say: "Number of internally displaced persons has not yet dropped" and that these persons were "being shifted locally by action of the security forces." Can you explain what you mean by this bullet point?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is the assessment that we could not observe that the numbers of IDPs dropped, but that they just moved around from -- just to avoid the fighting and that this is the assessment I make on the reports we got.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I tender 00564 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00484, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: May I call up 65 ter 557, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, in your statement you speak about a trip that you made to an area south of Komorane where you saw approximately 3.000 internally displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: South of Komorane.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Komorane, thank you. The document that is on the screen, that is 557, how does this relate to this trip that you made?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, I remember that we went with the Contact Group ambassadors we went to Kisna Reka, which is an IDP camp in the hills. And we went there, and I saw a camp where approximately a thousand people would live in the open.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And before we go into that, just to clarify, this report, who was it prepared by?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There are three authors, that is, mission chief, that means Mr. Petritsch; myself; and my colleague Mr. Senfter in Belgrade. So it's a joint report. I wrote the part of the IDP -- the visit to the IDP camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And that is set out in page 2, paragraph 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the IDPs that you saw when you visited the camp in Kisna Reka, that's in the second paragraph of -- under the heading IDP camps and possible repatriation. Two paragraphs below you say: "Apart from the destruction of their villages, the main reason why the displaced persons do not return home is the lack of security in the villages." Could you please explain what you meant by that statement.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, it's what the IDPs told us, that they don't feel secure to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did they explain why they did not feel secure to return?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, it continues in this same paragraph that they told us, they claimed, that when some villagers returned they were shot at or they were shot, three persons having died it says in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did they say who shot at them?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The way they portrayed it, of course, it was the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to look at item 3 in this document. It's headed "alleged massacre by security forces." And that is in page 3 of the English. In the second paragraph of item 3 you refer to an occurrence in Gornje Obrinje reported on by the ECMM and the media. Could you explain to us what this occurrence in Gornje Obrinje was?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. I saw photographs in the media. It was a -- in a ditch in Gornje Obrinje, IDP family which was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So this information was based on a report?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: On ECMM report, as it says in the brackets, ECMM and media.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. How about the incident referred to above in the village of Golubovac?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is where we with the Contact Group ambassadors went ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The main issue is that we -- Ambassador Petritsch, the undersigned, as it says, he and I, we saw a man who alleged that he survived a massacre on a group of young men.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another topic now, but if we could go back to the first page of 557, so the same document. At the second-last bullet point you refer to security coordinators in 70 villages. Could you explain what you mean by security coordinators?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was a project by Belgrade to set up -- they call it security coordinators or assistant policemen of local ethnic Albanian origin who were put into villages at -- in western Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Is this the same as the initiative you referred to in your statement where David Slinn travelled to Djakovica in 1998 to inquire about Serbian claims on local Albanian police force? This is in page 3, the last paragraph. I'm afraid we don't have your statement, but briefly it was a visit that David Slinn made to Djakovica around August 1999 to inquire about the Albanian police force. Is it the same issue, this Albanian police force, and the security coordinators referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same, and there were actually two trips, one I accompanied Mr. Slinn and the second I could not accompany him because I was dealing with the education agreement which was a totally different front in Kosovo. But he reported to me what he saw on this second trip where he was alone. And that was beginning of September, both trips.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Can I tender 65 ter 557 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00485, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we call up 65 ter 559, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, this is a document dated 7th of September, 1998. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And it's headed or it refers to the Kosovo local police plan of the Belgrade authorities. Can you explain the background to this specific document.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We went to this area to see by ourselves whether this claim that the local police force will be set up is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was your assessment?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That there were some attempts, certainly, at the first visit but we haven't seen it by ourselves; but on the second trip Mr. Slinn saw -- saw it by some people in uniforms but without side-arms yet and received a list of villages and persons being members of this local police force. But when he went to the villages after that from Djakovica, he did not find any of these people in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I tender 00559 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up 0 -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up 00558.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, this is a report dated the 20th of September, 1998, and it refers to the Kosovo local police force. Is this document related to the previous document that we saw?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. This is the follow-up visit by Mr. Slinn, which I said he made on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And just above the paragraph headed "verdict" right at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It should read "assessment," not verdict.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Assessment, thank you. The sentence above that reads: "Most villages were empty of inhabitants; only a very small number of people had returned even to Junik." What's the source of this information, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's Mr. Slinn.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you also refer to a cover-up operation right at the end of the document, this is at the end of the assessment paragraph. What do you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's also a mistranslation. I wrote in German "alibiaktion" so in the sense that we had a feeling it was not a serious -- serious move or attempt to create security by the locals themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00487, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Can we have 00556, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you draft this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I'm the author of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask some questions to clarify some points made in this document. On the issue of the security coordinators or local police that we have been talking about, if we look at paragraph 5 of page 1, this is towards the bottom of the page, the first bullet point that begins with the word "police." You say: " ... the Serbian side still appears to favour the model of 'security coordinators' ... " Could you explain this, please.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was -- in the brackets this is what my assessment is, that the Serbs still favour this model. I think it must have been -- must be in the context of international presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what do you mean by the context of international presence?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was the time there were intensive talks with Belgrade mainly done by the United States to -- to talk about models and -- both on the political side but also on the security side how to make arrangements to stabilise Kosovo and to get to the end of hostilities. And I think - that's what I now suspect - is that the Americans have proposed some international -- stronger international presence which would also give some sort of sense of security. And Belgrade probably tried to portray this model of local police, security coordinators, as being enough to assure the local Kosovo Albanian population that they were safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kickert. Before we leave this document, could we go to paragraph 2, also on page 1, where a reference is made to an IDP repatriation initiative. Is this the initiative you have been speaking to us about today?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Kisna Reka project. So there -- that's in the context there were two concrete projects, one was the return into Orahovac and the second one was the Kisna Reka return project.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00488, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Moving on to my final topic, Mr. Kickert. In your statement you refer to exhumations in Gornje Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 561, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page at the paragraph heading "forensic experts." The first bullet point you speak about individual international experts. Could you explain the background and context to this bullet point, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The whole issue of international forensic experts had to do with allegations from both sides of massacres, and the international community said, Well, we cannot rely on either side of the story, so what we would ask for is that independent international experts would look into these cases, and that was the whole idea which was already since June discussed with the Belgrade authorities. And here I just refer that Mr. Shattuck, who gave us a debrief, was cautiously optimistic that the Belgrade authorities might consider accepting individual international experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would like to tender 561 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could now have a look at 65 ter 560, please, at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Before we go there, do you recognise this document, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you prepare this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I'm the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 1 you refer to Mr. Sainovic being considered a close associate of the Yugoslav President Milosevic and him being taught to be responsible for coordinating the security forces. What was the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Him being present in Kosovo, and the source of information was the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could I take you to page 2 of this document, please, and the fourth bullet point from the bottom says: "Open with regard to dispatch of forensic medical experts." Is this related to the issue of international experts that you were just speaking about in relation to the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, that's the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And this document is dated the 7th of October, 1998. By this stage had any international experts entered Kosovo to carry out exhumations?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Not yet. It was -- at the beginning of October there were -- there was already -- I re-read that from another report - a call from the foreign policy advisor of President Milosevic, Mr. Bugarcic, to Mr. Petritsch, saying, yes, they would be willing to accept the Finnish forensic expert team, the team we, as the Austrian EU Presidency had proposed to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I think you refer to that matter in your statement. Could you explain what the outcome of this issue was, the access of the Finnish forensic team to exhume certain sites?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: In October it was -- the whole of October it was a back and forth on the mandate or the room of manoeuvre given to the Finnish team. Belgrade first wanted only to invite them through the Belgrade Forensic Institute; that was not enough for us. Then there came an exchange of letters between the Foreign Minister of the FRY, Mr. Jovanovic, and the Foreign Minister of Finland, Ms. Halonen, where an invitation, an official invitation was spelled out for the Finnish experts to come and make not only exhumations but just to come and talk to them on specific sites which would be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, when did you leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: During --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: During your various trips. You mentioned earlier that you made a number of trips to Kosovo during the summer and latter half of 1998. When was the last trip that you made to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, during our -- during the Austrian EU Presidency, the second half of 1998, I spent about half of my time in Kosovo and half of my time in Belgrade. I was -- in the beginning of 1999 I was also in Kosovo. Then in February we had the Rambouillet conference. Between the Rambouillet conference and the Paris conference I was also in Kosovo. And soon thereafter the NATO bombing started. I left the day -- in the morning, when in the evening the NATO bombing started.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge what was the outcome of the exhumations that were proposed in Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: During my time there, there were no exhumations of the Gornje Obrinje victims to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 561 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document under 00560 would be P00490.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you at this stage, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djordjevic, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Let me just prepare, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have several questions for you. You said that you didn't need your statement in writing before you, which was admitted as P478. I will have some questions concerning your statement. Mr. Kickert, before we start working on it, I would like to know, From the moment you left former Yugoslavia - and that would be the morning before the NATO bombing started in 1999, so the 24th of March - to date could you explain your diplomatic career for us?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. Thereafter we were in Vienna. Mr. Petritsch was still the Special Envoy of the European Union for Kosovo. He was then nominated to be the High Representative in Bosnia. After the NATO bombing, I myself returned to Kosovo, to Belgrade first and then to Kosovo. I opened up the Austrian office in Kosovo; was then political advisor to the SRSG of the UN mission in Kosovo, of Mr. Kouchner. After that I went to Canada on a posting and returned five years ago to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I read somewhere that you were advisor to Mr. Solana or representative of Mr. Solana's in Kosovo. I would like to know if that's true and something more about it.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. This was -- I was filling in for Fernando Gentilini. Fernando Gentilini had a car accident, must have been September 2004; and I filled in for three months in his position as personal representative of Javier Solana in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was your duty then? In other words, what was the purview of Mr. Gentilini, the person that you stood in for?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was mostly reporting to Brussels so that they had first-hand information. Therefore, I was in contact with Kosovo Albanian politicians, but I was also dealing with the Contact Group ambassadors. We had regular meetings to discuss the political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, concerning your statement to this Court that I mentioned, the first that you gave to representatives of this Court in Vienna. In paragraph 2 of your statement you say that your duty as the second secretary of the Austrian embassy at the time was to talk to politicians of Kosovo Albanians, intellectuals, and to maintain contacts with the parallel university at Pristina. You also said that you had frequent contacts with Albanian journalists. I would be interested in this: What was the purpose of your task, meaning maintaining contacts with ethnic Albanians and their institutions, and you mentioned the parallel university. We can agree that was a paralegal institution as well, can't we? So I would be interested to hear why were you tasked by your government, by your country, by your ambassador to perform those duties?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: On the parallel university, Austria has continued to recognise the parallel university as a university and has accepted the diplomas of this university. The rationale was after the autonomy was revoked we didn't want the Kosovo Albanian students to be punished doubly, A, that they didn't have their own university anymore; and B, that we -- they would not be recognised in Austria. So we had many Kosovo Albanian students who first studied in Pristina; and based on their diplomas from the parallel university, they were accepted to universities in Austria to final -- to finalise their studies. So one of my tasks was also to be in contact with the rectorate of the parallel university, to see whether these diplomas are correct, whether they really enrolled and made these diplomas because there was always a threat of forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And my next question would be: Didn't your diplomacy see this as interference into the internal affairs of a sovereign state such as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia being at the time. Can you imagine an opposite situation?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think the recognition of diplomas is mainly an issue of universities accepting diplomas of other universities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me, won't you, that contacts with paralegal institutions, including a university, within the framework of a sovereign state, is no business of Austria?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so. We were also in contacts with opposition figures. Why -- why wouldn't we be in contact with other institutions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that a second group of your tasks was to prepare the education agreement in Kosovo; am I right in saying so? Your answer is yes --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, no. No --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Or no?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The main interlocutors with Belgrade were -- was St. Edigio and Monsignor Paglia to discuss the education agreement. We came in from the European Union side because from the European commission we had projects to give money into the repair of some university premises. And there was a special group even tasked, and they stayed with us in the Austria house in Pristina to do this project because that summer there was an agreement that three buildings of the Pristina University would be given to the Kosovo Albanian students.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know after that agreement what was the conduct of the Kosovo Albanians with respect to the high education system? After that agreement was concluded, do you know whether those institutions started working; if not all of them, do you know which of them did since you were a direct participant in all that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I do recall that one of the big buildings at the technical faculty was never taken over and used. I think they also gave over the Institute of Albanology. That was used by -- by professors. And I think the -- if I'm not mistaken, there must have been the Faculty of Arts also given back to the Kosovo Albanians. I think this was also used. And then another project was dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Faculty of philosophy?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: "Filozofski," yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And given that you dealt with this matter, education, did you learn that there was a possibility to use the maternal tongue and listen to Jewish in mother tongue in official universities before the parallel system emerged?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge the Pristina University was a mixed-language university until the autonomy was revoked, and then it was mainly Serbian, since 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it was only in Serbian, that there was no possibility for Albanian classes? Do you know what it's all about? Do you have any direct personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: If you ask me whether I was hearing classes, no; I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What would be the source of your information in this respect? Maybe the rector of the parallel university or persons of that sort or any official institution maybe?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, I also had a meeting with the -- with the Serbian rector of the university in Pristina, and he was very much against any education in Albanian. He says, This is Serbia, they should learn Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will agree that Serbian had to be the official language, but I will not be able to agree with you that the use of Albanian language was denied in the then-institution of high education of Serbia. I would like to ask you whether you know that there were Albanian classes in primary and secondary education? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you've said that Austria as a state, that you represented as a diplomat, that was concerned over the rescission of autonomy and that you maintained contacts, as you state in paragraph 2 of your statement. I would like to be interested to hear before establishing contacts with the parallel university in Pristina with Kosovo Albanian intellectuals, politicians, journalists that you were personally involved in, did Austria conduct talks with official Serbian institutions and their politicians concerning this matter? So before you established contacts that you described in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, it was usual practice that when we would go down to Pristina to meet Kosovo Albanians, we'd also meet Veljko Odalovic, the prefect in Pristina. That was standard practice, so -- and it was everybody, every diplomat who went to Pristina did the same -- did a little circus of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Which function was performed by Veljko Odalovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We had known him as the prefect of Kosovo, but I think he was of a certain "okrug," group, the head of it. But he was the representative in Pristina, and so because the trips we diplomats usually took just took us to Pristina, we would see him. Later on there was also Minister Andjelkovic who was in Pristina, and we would also see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you addressed to those persons by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the time or by some of the competent politicians that you conducted talks at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, we would establish contact directly with their offices and make appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement you say that you went to Kosovo in January 1998, as you confirmed today; and you said that in the autumn of 1998, after the Serb offensive against the KLA, you say that your efforts in Kosovo ensued from the prevailing conflict between the Serbs and the Kosovo Albanians. I would like, given that the transcript does not contain what you meant to say on that occasion, could you please explain what you mean by the prevailing conflict between the Serbs and the Kosovo Albanians. Do you see it as a conflict between the Serbs and the Albanians or a conflict between the then-established KLA, the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, and the Serb security forces, do you see it as a legitimate action of Serb security forces against outlaws or faction of a certain group; or do you really mean a conflict between Serbs and the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: When I came to Belgrade to the Austrian embassy in November 1997, there were already an intensifying string of reports of incidents in Kosovo. When I first went down to Kosovo, I just went to Pristina; I was introduced by a Swedish democrat who used to go more frequently and for years down to Kosovo and also to -- outside of Pristina; and then with the -- with the events, a situation escalated. If you say -- if you ask me whether there was a conflict between the Serbs and the Kosovo Albanians, I say no. It was a conflict between KLA, if you can call them armed elements, and security forces. Where the civilian population was dragged in, we have many allegations, maybe that's what you want to refer to, is of abductions at the time. We -- people in Kosovo at that time, there was little interaction between the ethnic groups. Shkelzen Maliqi an intellectual wrote two -- "Separate Worlds." They were living next to each other but not with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is the right time for the technical break, given that's it's past 10.30. So I would stop with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Yes, we need now to break for half an hour. I think you're a little used to the system, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By now, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kickert, we left off citing the words of Mr. Shkelzen Maliqi concerning the relationship between the Serbian and the Albanian people. When I say "the Albanian people," I mean the Albanians living in Kosovo and Metohija, since Mr. Shkelzen Maliqi was born there as well. And you mentioned, answering my question, that the civilian population was dragged into the conflict. Please, try to explain to me what you meant by saying that the civilian population got involved into this conflict and what you meant by it, given that you had good information about the nature of the conflict that was prevailing in that area?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Can I describe for the number of IDPs this was a direct consequence of the fighting between the KLA and the security forces. The same time when I described the civilian with a Kalashnikov in a village on the main road, Pristina-Pec. It's not by coincidence; he must have felt insecure that he had to carry a gun with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Those civilians that you saw with Kalashnikovs, which ethnic group did they belong?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was one person in a Serbian village, but I didn't stop and talk to him. But my guess is since it was a Serbian village it was a Serbian civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that members of the KLA, with respect to the civilians of the towns and villages where their combat operations were underway against the Serb security forces, that they had removed and moved those civilians in those areas away to safety?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There were certain allegations. Whether they had moved them away or forced them to leave, this was -- I was asked the last time I was witnessing here, and I cannot say what was the correct thing. But the fact was that civilian population was moving, there were many in the open. For whatever reason, they stayed in the open. When asking them, they told us that they felt insecure because of the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is not coincidental, since you were a person authorised by the -- your embassy to talk to the persons that you mentioned in your statement. My question was direct: Do you know that within the framework of the guerilla or terrorist tactics of the KLA army, was it their strategy and tactics to remove civilian or ask civilians to move to a safer place before they launched their attacks. Whether you had such information or not, this is my question.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information about the situation where after combat operations members of the KLA would intermingle with the civilian population in the area where they had undertaken offensive actions, did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, I think that's general guerilla tactics, but what I can tell you is when I was visiting the IDP camp in Kisna Reka, I think it was two or three times there, at one occasion I did -- ran into a KLA in uniform, KLA soldier in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As a diplomat of a country presiding over the European Union and person in frequent contacts with the most powerful countries in the world and maintaining contacts with powerful military alliances -- but my question to you as a diplomat who frequently visited Kosovo in -- starting from January 1998, do you know that the KLA was treated and considered as a terrorist organisation at the time? Do you have such information; and if so, could you tell us what you knew about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was called terrorist organisation by Belgrade, and I think at one occasion even the US Envoy Gelbard used this term, but in general this term was tried to avoid it by the internationals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I can understand your answer because you yourself stated that you had contacts with the KLA and their politicians and that they asked them to organise themselves so that they could have a single Albanian platform for negotiations. Do you consider your activities inappropriate in terms of diplomatic activities in the territory of a foreign country?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. The whole idea was to get the KLA into the political process. This was the reason why we met with the KLA. Because we saw the situation escalating and what we were fearing was a destabilisation of Kosovo and the region and which would have repercussions to us. As you are aware, there are many Kosovo Albanian refugees in western European countries, including my own, and we had no interest that this number would increase.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know today as a diplomat that anybody is investing efforts to reach any arrangements with the leading terrorist organisations to try to make them a part of the main stream or of a process.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Time and again this is part of diplomacy, whether that's the Hezbollah in Lebanon, whether it's the Hamas in the Gaza Strip, whether it's the FARK in Colombia, time and again diplomats are in contact with, whatever you want to call them -- rebel groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now things seem clearer to me. My next question is going to concern part of your testimony today during your examination-in-chief conducted by my learned friend. You mentioned Pec, you mentioned internally displaced person, and you mentioned a village by the name of Istinic. You said that there were 20, 25.000 internally displaced persons. Would you agree with me when I say that the village of Istinic at the time was controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: At that certain moment I cannot tell you. I know that this was an area where there was intense fighting going on between the KLA and the security forces, but I couldn't say at that particular moment whether it was controlled by KLA, this village, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the source of your information concerning Istinic, your direct observations during your outing there, or did you receive regular reports from European Monitoring Mission, Contact Group representatives, and other NGOs?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I was not myself there. Having read the report, we got regular ECMM reports, European monitors, and this particular case I cite the Dutch military attache who gave me his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You are right when you say that fierce fighting was going on there, but the village of Istinic was at the time under KLA control and this is why ethnic Albanians sought refuge there. You do not know that, but do you know that those Albanians would later return to their homes after Serb security forces managed to enter the village of Istinic and maintain a degree of control for a time? Do you have such information from the sources that you just cited, not necessarily the Dutch embassy, but other sources as well?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I can't recall them now, but in other cases there were also -- like, as I mentioned, Orahovac, there were returns which also tried to facilitate into areas which were controlled by Serb security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Orahovac. Do you know who actually caused the conflict in Orahovac on the 17th, the 18th, and the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. I'm just -- I just thought a little bit more carefully because a few days after, I did go to Malisevo and -- so I wouldn't know what happened these days, but I heard a story that the KLA tried to enter Orahovac and based on that the offensive started and the KLA had to abandon Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that what you heard, that the KLA attacked Orahovac, do you know that they actually took Orahovac; and do you know that they killed and kidnapped a number of people, that those people were taken to prison in Malisevo, the place that you just mentioned? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that occasion Zyrapi, the witness who -- whom we have heard recently, and Mr. Thaqi were actually in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the KLA attacked Opterusa, that's the name of the place, and that it took ten men and nine women to the prison in Malisevo. The women were taken to Sali Revkija's [phoen] shop and were sexually molested. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I see that your memory is selective. So did anyone in the Austrian embassy have as his or her task contacts with Serbs? And this involves some really key events. And you were drafting reports that came in from the European monitors, and I actually went through many of those reports. So I'm asking you that how come that you don't have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The monitors were often not given access to areas where there were fights going on. They had, like I, to pass check-points. And if they were not allowed to continue, they could not write reports, like you said, on the Opterusa case. Of course we were in contact with both sides. The whole operation, the whole idea, of the monitors were that they would look into allegations from both sides and try to verify them. I -- talking about Orahovac, after regaining the control of Orahovac there were allegations of mass graves in Orahovac, where we sent - allegations by the Kosovo Albanians - where we sent specifically our ECMM monitors to go there and report. And they said, Well, this was again exaggeration by the Kosovo Albanians. There were some grave-sites, indeed, at a waste dump, but it was certainly was not a mass grave as described in their allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 17th of July the KLA attacked Retimlje, took it, that they took 15 Serb civilians prisoner, and transported them to the prison in Malisevo and they have never been seen since? Do you have any knowledge of that event? So it's approximately the same time-period, this major offensive launched by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about -- well, I think it was the 21st of July that the KLA members attacked the village of Zociste, looted it, burnt down the houses, and expelled all the Serbs who had been living there. Do you have any knowledge of that incident in any way, any kind of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. There was just general knowledge of these allegations that Serb civilians were abducted. On that, yes, but on -- concretely on Zociste, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will now take you back to an earlier period, the Pristina-Pec road. Do you know that on the 18th of June the traffic along this road was cut off in the place of Iglarevo? Near Klina a roadblock was set up from the Pec side, and from the Pristina side a roadblock was set up near Lapusnik, it's the Glogovac municipality. Did you receive such a report from the monitors? Do you have any knowledge of that, about this road being blocked, both from the Pristina and from the Pec side?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I have knowledge that the road was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, what do you know about the village of Kijevo and the KLA activities? What do you know? When I say "Kijevo," what does that make you think of? Does that jog your memory in any way?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, the famous Holbrooke sentence: Kijevo, the most dangerous place on earth. It was a mostly Serbian- and I think also Roma-inhabited village which was cut off from the surrounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you just saved a question regarding Ambassador Holbrooke, but do you know that this village was blockaded; and if you do, for how long after the KLA attack?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I know it was cut off, blockaded as you call it; but I do not know for which period. But it must have been a suspended period because it was at that time pretty much an issue which was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be quite sufficient. My next question regarding the KLA activities and the reporting from various NGOs and monitors of the European Commission. Do you know anything about the attack on the Obilic thermal power-plant? It's the late spring or early summer of that year, 1998, and do you know that some employees working there at the power-plant were abducted by the KLA in the summer of 1998? Do you have any knowledge of that? So first of all the attack in the late spring/early summer; and the second question is the kidnapping of the nine employees of the Obilic thermal power-plant. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I have no knowledge that the thermal power-plant itself was attacked, but the surroundings of Obilic. And I think what I referred to, Belacevac, maybe that's the one you also wanted to refer to, but I know that's very near and that could be the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Belacevac is fine, but I'm talking about the thermal power-plant and one part that was attacked by the KLA. So that was my question. Do you have any knowledge; and if yes, what knowledge, what do you know about Belacevac? You mentioned it after all.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I don't have a recollection of an attack on the Obilic power-plant, and Belacevac I was mentioning because this was in my report when I said that Mr. Odalovic said it in the end of June that -- officially the first time that VJ was involved in inland operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about kidnapping of the nine employees who were on the company bus or van, whatever it was, they were kidnapped by the KLA and have never been seen since or their remains were found? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There were many reports of abducted people, could also be this one. I also remember that even a Russian journalist was abducted; he was freed, though. It was a time when there were many allegations of abductions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge of the kidnapping of the nine workers who worked in the Obilic thermal power-plant, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: If I would look through my documents and would find it there, I could refresh my memory; but if you ask me now directly whether I remember, I cannot with certainty say yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm quite satisfied with the answer that I got. Please tell me, do you know anything about illegal, semiprivate prisons that were run by the KLA where they kept non-Albanians? Do you have any knowledge; and if so, what knowledge do you have?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: At the time there were these allegations and more information about them I only got when I was hear as a witness in the Limaj et al case.
