utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I read that part, the -- His Honour Judge Parker was on that case too, but could you please remind me because I can't recall now, what kind of knowledge? What was the source?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: These were the same spirit as the allegations were of kidnappings and killings of civilians, there were also allegations which you would also find in the press, in the media, of detention camps which the KLA had. But we had no first-hand information, and at that time in June we didn't have the observers, the monitors, in larger numbers. We had one team from the end of May which is two persons, and they could only go where, A, the security was enough and where they were not stopped by roadblocks, either by the Serbian security forces or the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not my impression that the monitors did not go to dangerous areas. My impression was, in fact, quite the opposite. The only question was the physical ability of reaching some areas. For instance, you mentioned Malisevo many times. But let me ask you this: Did you ever go to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- yeah, I would have to think when exactly, but I went to Lapusnik, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you're much more familiar with Malisevo than with Lapusnik, you went there much more often, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about any camps or prisons, prison camps, set up by the KLA in Malisevo and in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Again, the only -- not concretely, just generally, the rumours that there were some camps. And when I was in Malisevo there was also the ICRC, same what I was looking for, a responsible person to talk to on the KLA for the political side, they tried to contact somebody in the KLA to talk about these allegations. And also when we talked to them, we would -- we would ask them to follow international humanitarian law rules which -- also, because of these allegations, we brought them up with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you talk to from the political -- from the top political wing people in the KLA as you describe them?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: At the time we had no knowledge of how the KLA was organised. So what we tried was to get in contact, the first contacts, and to see who they would represent to us as their spokesperson, as a decision-maker, and that was the from -- must have been the 22nd of July, since I've read my reports again, when Mr. Rohan came we went to Malisevo, and then the day after, 23rd it must have been, I met Mr. Thaqi, which I didn't know it was Mr. Thaqi at the time because they themselves introduced only by numbers to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Thaqi number one? Who was number one?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, it was -- he was number three.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Who was number one?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I don't know until today. Maybe it was Mr. Adem Jashari. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Maybe we won't. Do you know about any other numbers? Three, that's Hashim Thaqi. Two, four, five, six, do you remember? That's how it was, yes. You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, of course. The number seven, the one we saw first, Mr. Kadri Veseli I learned later on; he was number seven. And in one of my later reports I was speculating Jakup Krasniqi being number 11 or 12. But we were sort of all of us a little bit in the dark on the organisational structure of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever met Zyrapi? Yes? No?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall at this moment, Zyrapi, that's the last name that I know him by. He was the -- he was also a commander in the KLA -- well obviously you don't remember since you're asking for his first name -- and his name is actually Bislim, Bislim Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but I don't know in which context. I've certainly not at that time met him by name. Certainly not by name. Where was he commander, in which area?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now we're getting beyond the context of the questions that I'm dealing with now, so we'll stop here. My next question: When did you learn that Mr. Hashim Thaqi was number three? When did you learn that Mr. Veseli was number seven? What time in relation to the time when you knew them only as three and seven respectively?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: They introduced themselves as -- at the meeting itself as number seven and Hashim Thaqi as number three. So we just knew at that time just the numbers, no names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When did you learn their names and what they actually were, who those numbers actually designated?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I learned the name of Mr. Thaqi rather fast after the meeting with him because the journalist who brought me there was a friend of his from university time. So that's how I got to contact him in the first place. But I kept it -- I didn't even put it into my reports. And about, I don't know, late summer it was public knowledge, it was also in Kosovo Albanian media, his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your frequent contacts with the Serbian authorities, did you hear from them about Mr. Thaqi -- well, I'm just now going to limit myself to him. I'm not going to ask you questions about anyone else. And if yes, what is it that they told you about him?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: If his name was mentioned, it was also in late summer, and he was labelled as -- probably as a leading terrorist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably or for sure?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now it's much clearer. Mr. Thaqi, or rather, Mr. Three, did he introduce himself by saying, I'm number three and my powers, my authority, my function is such and such? Did he tell you what he was in charge of, and why is it that he is the one talking to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He introduced himself as number three, but he didn't state what he was responsible for. I said we were looking for high leaders of the KLA to introduce them to the political process, and he said, We are willing to consider that. But he did not say whether he had to ask somebody else or that he would decide on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You know, diplomacy is a very delicate matter; you will agree with me as an experienced diplomat. I could say as an intelligence officer -- well, you might agree with me or not. But did it occur to you that number three might be a Serbian mole? How could you be so sure that here is a representative of that organisation that was labelled terrorist by the other side and they wanted to -- and he wanted to talk to you about it their future activities?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, I mean if you're in a city like Malisevo and you see nobody else but KLA and no Serbian security forces, you would assume that he is from the KLA. And I was -- before I was led through to him I was questioned by a different gentleman in a cafe. He was clearly sounding me out, trying to establish whether I was really a diplomat and serious. As many were returning from German-speaking countries, I could communicate directly in German with them. And this person who was sounding me out, it was about certainly an hour that I was questioned before I was allowed to meet Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This gentleman who questioned you -- well, who brought you to him, the journalist that you mentioned or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The journalist. We went to Malisevo. There we were seated. Then this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Dukadjin?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Dukadjin, Gorani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Correct. [Interpretation] My next question: Did this gentleman introduce himself by number or by name and did he tell you who he was when he talked to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He had a nickname and introduced himself as -- with his nickname, and let me just think what his nickname was -- Hoxha?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Hoxha, very well. Did he tell you what his function was, that he was a member of the KLA, that he was a security officer in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think he told me he was a security officer. He was not in uniform, he was in civilian clothes, whereas Thaqi when I met him and Veseli, they had uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: What other officials of the KLA or of the parallel political hierarchy of the Kosovo Albanian government did you meet, either alone or as part of various delegations that went there, what politicians, what officers of the KLA possibly? And, for instance, intellectuals, journalists. In a word, key figures that you deemed to be persons that you should contact. Either -- it was either your opinion or the opinion of the people that you worked with.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Our primary interlocutors were the politicians in Pristina, the LDK, Ibrahim Rugova, Fehmi Agani, then many others in the LDK. Then there was a group which split off from the LDK, Mehmet Hajrizi, there were others in this group, Qosja, and also -- so we had contacts with the LDK; the splinter faction, which was in opposition to the LDK; and then as a third pillar, the KLA outside, which was very difficult to meet because, A, we didn't know who were the right interlocutors; and B, then because of the fighting and they would move. So it was after two meetings in Malisevo I had, as you are aware, the meeting in Klecka with Jakup Krasniqi, Ram Buja, and Fatmir Limaj, together with my British colleague David Slinn and thereafter we had lost contact because they moved somewhere else. And it was not until we had -- until late summer, September, that we had contact, but it was only via phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We have understood what you were doing for your country and in what way. But from your testimony I garnered that you did not do that as Austria, not even as the European Union, but in the broadest sense of the word in terms of diplomatic activity of the USA and the European Union. I want to know who else - I don't mean persons but states - who was involved in those joint activities that also involved Austria, either through you or through Ambassador Petritsch, in observing and monitoring the situation in Kosovo? Who were the key players, what states?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I mean, the key state was United States. In KDOM, Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Missions, there was -- there were many components, or three main components, one was the US component, the second one was the European component, and then there was also a Russian component. And there were also joint trips into the country-side. There was also a Canadian car, one team from Canada I remember -- yeah, that's it. Then the Contact Group, of course, as I explained, they are the main political formation where Mr. Hill, the -- at that time the ambassador -- the US ambassador to Skopje was designated as the Special Envoy for Kosovo. We didn't have, on the European side, anybody yet, and we were accused of inaction, inactivity, even ridiculed at times. And it was only until September that Ambassador Petritsch was named Special Envoy and formalised at the foreign ministers' meeting in early October only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The working of the international community you just described through what countries it was implemented. I want to know about the coordination. You mentioned European Union, the USA, and the Russian Federation as the key players. Now I want to know about the interaction, their interaction, not in formal terms, but substantively. What was the cooperation like between the Russians and the EU, the Americans and the EU, Americans and Russians. So not formally because we all know what it looked like on the surface, formally. But I want you to try and answer this question for me because you are the right person. You can tell me what their relationship was like in the actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: You had various initiatives and the interaction was either formal meetings, Contact Group ambassadors would meet or they would give briefings, so if Mr. Hill saw a high-ranking Serbian politician he would tend to debrief us afterwards, he would not include us, but he would debrief us. The Russians also sent somebody down, Afanasievsky, if I'm not mistaken, to -- so that the Russians would also talk to -- in Belgrade to the politicians and say, We need to do something, this here is escalating. They did participate as I said in KDOM. So there was a joint cooperation in -- on all levels, whether that was the diplomatic level or the monitor level. There were joint reports by the monitors, there were joint outings by the monitors. And they would then also important to put some basic information to New York on Security Council Resolution 1199, whether that was kept or not or honoured. So I think their -- they did give different inputs, the three different -- the Americans, the Europeans, and the Russians, input to New York. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Partly, but thank you anyway. My next question: You did say that the most important country in this whole process were the United States of America. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me now, are you familiar with the oath that members of the KLA or perspective members of the KLA had to take while entering that military organisation? Do you know the text of their oath?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As a diplomat, did number three, that is, Mr. Thaqi; number seven, Mr. Veseli; and the other numbers that we can't recall, did they tell you what their political goals were and how they intend to go about realising them? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I mean, their -- they even stated it publicly, Mr. Jakup Krasniqi, as a spokesperson, that independence was their goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But how did they intend to go about achieving that independence?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: By military means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what were the goals, the reported goals, of the most important and strongest political party, Mr. Rugova's party, what did he say about his goals?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The same, independence. But he -- sorry. But he was committed to peaceful means and sort of the whole in our assessment is that there was a lot of impatience by some circles of the Kosovo Albanian community that this way Rugova took -- will not lead to anything, and this is why you had one political faction breaking away from Mr. Rugova who wanted to have a more proactive way. And then you had the KLA who chose the military way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this faction which split off from Rugova. Was the method of achieving independence was armed struggle or something else? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The splinter faction was also political means, not military means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for them going their own road because it's the same goal and the same method of achieving it?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: They wanted to have a more active approach, making demonstrations, and like in the Kosovo Albanian political spectrum you always have different fractions, and it was very difficult - and this was one of our aims - is to get these fractions together because who would be able to talk to Belgrade on what we were at the time working on some autonomy if they would not represent the whole spectrum of the Kosovo Albanians or, like the LDK, would be not willing to go it alone because they said, We have no influence over the KLA. How could they negotiate something with Belgrade which would include a secession of hostilities if they had no influence on those, meaning the KLA, who did engage in the hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your ambassador at the time, Mr. Petritsch, and the UK ambassador and the American ambassador to Skopje and to Belgrade, the Russian Federation's ambassador to Belgrade, they all conducted talks with the political elite of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. I'm not going to specify Mr. Milosevic and his closest associates. I'm not going to mention the top brass of Montenegro. But I would like to call them collectively the political elite of the FRY of the time. I've no -- listed the ambassadors of the countries which I see as key -- being key in that process. What I'm interested in is was there a single unified diplomatic stance at one place concerning the problem of Kosovo and Metohija and autonomous province within the Republic of Serbia, one of two, and within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whether there was a common stance with respect to the political efforts invested by the political elite of Serbia at the time and whether they were amenable to peaceful negotiations with the Albanians; and if not, why not? What was the crux of the political stance of the political elite of Serbia as assessed by international diplomats because you were there in this hot spot at the time? What are your impressions and your knowledge generally speaking? This is what I'm getting at .

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The lead clearly were with the United States and with Mr. Hill. There was also an initiative, so if that's what you're aiming at -- there were various initiatives. One was certainly Mr. Hill who was -- who had lead, then the Russians, with Mr. Afanasievsky, also tried to talk to the leadership. The European Union at that time didn't play a role yet. As I said, Mr. Petritsch was at that early stage in summer nothing but the EU Presidency ambassador. I -- if I may recall, the OSCE and the EU had a double-hatted envoy for ex-Yugoslavia, Mr. Gonzales, if I'm not mistaken, and he was virtual impossible to perform his duties because he was not given a visa to enter the FRY, and this was the -- one of the reasons Mr. Petritsch was picked as a Special Envoy of the European Union because he could not be denied a visa because he was already on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There were certain internal political reasons why Mr. Gonzales was denied a visa. You will agree with me. The authorities had reasons to deny him the visa, he was a persona non grata at the time. What I'd like to hear, whether the attitude of the ambassadors and the reports that they sent to their respective countries and governments was that the Serbian authorities are trying, through negotiations and in a peaceful manner, to resolve all problems concerning Kosovo and Metohija, or was it different? This is the gist of the whole matter concerning that period of time. Do you know what was the explanation of -- proffered by the Serb authorities about why the Serb security forces, why the Serb army, was there on the ground? What was the thinking and the opinion of foreign ambassadors about that problem at the time about the position of the Serb government, Serbian government, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Belgrade saw it, the whole Kosovo issue, as an internal issue. And as you also accused me of meddling into internal issues. And their opposition towards a greater role, was they didn't want to internationalise the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: They did not?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: They did not want to have it internationalised. We -- remember, we had OSCE long-term mission before also in Kosovo and Sandzak also and -- which was terminated. And the idea was to have an international mission there to stabilise it, being there so that things would not escalate. And that was so that the thinking from the KDOM led into the Kosovo Verification Mission which -- in October. So the idea was to be present there to stabilise things and not have them getting out of the hand, and one part of it was also to establish a political process where Belgrade and Pristina or, if you like, the Kosovo Albanians with Serb authorities would talk about the future status of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, I absolutely understand your position, and I appreciate your service. I know that you're a cog wheel in the mechanism of your government who does what he's told. I'm not accusing you of anything. You have to share the prevailing opinion of your government. It's nothing personal. But let's move on. Using your rich experience in the field, now you're entering a contradiction when you say, We have monitoring missions, I'm not going to list them all to save time, OSCE, KDOM, European monitors, a Contact Group, and tens of NGOs. That doesn't fit with your claim that there was no -- that the issue was not internationalised, this issue of Kosovo and Metohija, by the Serb government and that they had not allowed that. Could you please disentangle this illogic stance that you have.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: For me it's not illogic at all, but the international presence, of course there were international NGOs working in the humanitarian field. There was at the time when I went down from 1998 on there was a US information office but nothing else. I was among the few diplomats who would go down to Kosovo regularly. There were just periodic visits by ambassadors, and they only went to -- mostly to Pristina. There were two colleagues, one from the British, one from the Swedish embassy, who would deal more intensively, but there was hardly any international presence there in Pristina. When we agreed on KDOM, and interestingly enough this D came in on the insistence of Belgrade to call it diplomatic, and all these monitors had to be accredited by the -- by the -- by their embassies of their nationality and they were not allowed to have the EU umbrella because that's going too far. So they were always on their national capacity. Of course we organised them as the EU jointly, but the wish of the Belgrade authorities was not having too much of an international presence. That's also why they denied the European Union to have -- house a presence there. And that's the reason why we in our national capacity rented a house in Pristina which we would sublet to European institutions, like ECHO, the humanitarian office, to make some sort of hub for the EU there. That was in July of 1998. But the whole effort, we also -- as I told you before, we had a lack of information and being present we wanted to have our own sources of information and not rely on allegations and counter-allegations. And as I wrote in my report when we went to Decani, inflating news and -- I say, well, what the LDK claims is nonsense, it's not a second Vukovar, because we were dependent because we had no presence on the ground on what other sources, open sources, we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I could gather is that eventually there were many monitoring missions in Kosovo. What Ambassador Hill was doing there, the Dutch ambassador was there, Ambassador Walker was there. Had they not been there, there would not have been the reports that you received at different times from different places in Kosovo. But let's move on to a different line of questioning. I'd like to honour my promise that I will finish your cross-examination today because of your obligations. My question is going to concern your statement, your 1999 statement, taken in Vienna. You said - that would be paragraph 4: "In March 1998 members of the diplomatic corps were taken by the Yugoslav Ministry of Foreign Affairs to Prekaz in Kosovo to show them what the KLA had done there. The Austrian government did not send a representative on this trip because we did not want to be used as a pawn in a propaganda campaign." Of course doesn't say by whom, but it can be concluded that it would be the propaganda launched by the Serbian or Yugoslav government. I would like you to comment on your obviously personal opinion of this.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was a decision by all the EU countries not to participate in this particular outing. We changed our opinion, I'll tell you then why. But why do I talk about propaganda? Because when you're there you see the embassy representatives, see the footage, and then the caption is the story which one side gives. And they would say, Okay, we were taken to see by ourselves the terrorist hideouts and so on. That there was an allegation that -- that sort of a massacre happened there, and we didn't want to be misused to go there. The disadvantage was that we couldn't see by our own. Military attaches then went to this area, but we, as diplomats, not yet. And that's the reason we said at the second offer to Decani that we would take this offer up and go there so that we could see by ourselves what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The very claim that it went for a propaganda campaign launched by the Serbian government automatically begs the question of your credibility seen through the eyes of the Defence team in this case. Since you took this stance in an uncompromising manner, I can conclude from that - and you've explained it a bit better - but for it to be clear to everybody in the courtroom, I will have to ask you the next question. What was the quantity and extent of your knowledge about what had happened at that location at Prekaz in Kosovo, the place you were invited to by the Serbian government -- or I mean the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Did you have information about that; if so, from whom, and what was the content of that information?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I did have information from my then-British and -Swedish colleague who went there the day after it had happened. They saw it by themselves and reported it to me. Later on I also remember I saw photographs of the victims which were laid out in Srbica, Skenderaj, taken by the deputy defence attache of Germany, and they were also in the newspapers, the Kosovo Albanian newspapers, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I see that you remember that. What was -- what were the name of the colleagues that informed you about Prekaz, those who went there the day after. Could you please supply us with their names?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The Swedish colleague was called Jonas Weiss and the British colleague Julian Braithwaite.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall their positions, what were their titles in their embassies?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The Swedish colleague was, like myself, I think second secretary, had the similar portfolio as I did; and Mr. Braithwaite maybe was first secretary but certainly not -- like myself, a junior diplomat at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was he in charge exclusively of Kosovo, I mean Mr. Braithwaite, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, he also dealt with media affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question concerning your answer will be as follows: What kind of information they relayed to you the day after the Prekaz event? What did they tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: They told me about the destruction of the compound, which I've only seen much later, and that apparently there were some heavier -- heavier guns or -- used to perform this sort of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What did the Serb authorities determine in connection with Prekaz at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That they have taken out a terrorist stronghold. I even remember that that very day of Prekaz, the German ambassador was seeing Mr. Odalovic; and during the meeting somebody came in and told Mr. Odalovic something and he turned to the German ambassador and said that, The terrorist issue is solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Between receiving those two pieces of information, the one you received by the Swedish and British colleague and that received by the -- from the Serbian government, did you have any other information concerning Prekaz incidents? Do you have any personal knowledge about Prekaz gleaned from other sources?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I didn't have any personal experience from Prekaz at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your colleagues arrived there the day after the skirmish at Prekaz and they reported seeing destruction, damage?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I -- maybe it was the day after or maybe even the same day because I think it was in the early morning this action, and they had slipped in, I don't know through which way, to Prekaz. And they told me also that when they returned on the normal road that the Serbian police was taken by surprise that they were there, and I think that they were even taken into custody briefly. But -- yeah, that's what they told me, and I think that the next day they returned to Belgrade. That's when I was informed by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: They were detained? They were not put into custody? There is a significant difference in those two terms. Custody is a very strong measure. Maybe it is a matter of interpretation. This is what I heard in my headphones. So they were detained --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- for a while to check and verify?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: -- could be questioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not up to you or up to me. This is the interpretation that I heard. I do not follow the transcript at the same time. I rely on what I hear. Concerning this information we can conclude - and will you agree with me - that there was a conflict, that it happened there between Serb security forces, whichever forces they may be, and the KLA, which in the eyes of the Serb government at the time was a terrorist organisation? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The problem with Prekaz and why it became such a big thing is because many family members were killed as well from the Jasharis. So you had these pictures of women and children, dead women and children as well, and you didn't have the sort of what we later saw, the classical uniformed KLA against Serbian security forces. I don't recall that any one of those victims had any kind of insignia on them. I know that we were presented or the military attache were presented with weaponry found there. This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that a conflict had taken place there between the KLA and the Serb security forces; did I understand you correctly now or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I would be cautious stating that because it was very different to what happened in summer, where it appeared that it was much more organised, the KLA. Here it was an action to a family compound and if -- and now in the aftermaths we know that Mr. Jashari was an important member of the KLA, but not necessarily between the KLA only as such and the police forces. I think it was an attack on a compound of somebody who belonged to the KLA but involved many other family members at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear who Mr. Adem Jashari was?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, now he's heralded by the KLA as the founding father of the KLA, the legendary leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that had been warrants for arrest, that there had been investigations undertaken against him because of his work against the constitutional order of the republic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that several Serb police officers were killed and injured there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. There were, since I arrived in Belgrade, reports of attacks on police cars, escorts -- so, yes, I'm aware of that. And also killings of individuals. I remember a case of a woodworker who was killed and that was in the village of Drenica area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serb security forces called on them to surrender to get out peacefully? Do you know that? Do you know that Adem Jashari refused to do that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that -- do you know what Adem Jashari's house looked like? Have you ever seen it, the house where he lived? Do you know what the walls, the ramparts around his house looked like? There were embrasures there. It was a veritable fortress. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know the compound -- later, I did see it, yeah. But sort of the way it is now with the destructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, you say that you know that Serb police officers were killed there. Well, I don't know if the interpreter will be able to interpret that properly, but they were not killed by slingshots. They were killed by fire-arms. Did you see the fire-arms that he had in his house, and will you agree with me that the fire-arms are not what is considered to be personal weapons, side-arms? Those were hand-grenades, heavy machine-guns? And after this question my last question, because I can see that you are confirming that by nodding, but I would like to hear you say yes for the record. Is it logical then that now that we've agreed about that that you are labelling this Serbian propaganda? Can you imagine the very same situation, for instance, in your own country? There's a crazy Slovene, a Corinthian Slovene -- I'm quite familiar with this because I see Slovenia to this day as my former country, my homeland, and now you have an Adem Jashari and he decides to gain independence for the Slovenian minority in Austria. Would it then be Austrian propaganda if your state were to take any measures against such a man or do you think it is his democratic right to arm himself with mines, heavy machine-gun, hand-grenades, and to open fire on the Austrian security forces? That's why I'm asking you: Why did you say that you didn't want to be a pawn in the hands of the Serbian propaganda? I see this as a tragic event and this is something that I find really very upsetting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I apologise, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are making an extremely lengthy political speech, including in it a great deal of factual substance. If you want the witness to comment on a particular matter, raise it, in a short manner, directly --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, you're right, of course, Your Honour. Your Honour, you're absolutely right. I just wanted to ask why is this labelled propaganda if we have this state of affairs? And I do apologise for making this lengthy speech. It was not politically motivated, believe me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First to answer beginning of your statement. Yes, we were presented with the weaponry - that's what I mentioned before - and it is certainly not side-arms or hunting rifles, but far from that. Point one. Point two, you had two allegations on this Prekaz thing. One was that it was a legitimate police action against terrorists, the other one was that it was a massacre on a family. I'm aware of the fact that apparently Mr. Jashari was asked to give himself up, and he refused to, and that was the reason for the attack on Prekaz. On the, if I may, on the political issue. The situation was that the province of Kosovo had substantial autonomy which was revoked. So there is not -- there is an avenue where we wanted to get the political leaders of Kosovo, engage with Belgrade to agree on circumstances where they would be willing to live in a common state of the future. Why didn't we want to be sent there? As I said, propaganda. You would be just sent there and with the footing you would just get one side of the story and not the other one. And that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Have you ever been to Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there via Lipovac, the road that goes through the village of Lipovac, or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Lipovac or Likovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Likovac, Likovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. I've been to Likovac, also must have been a few times, because it was also one of headquarter of the KLA; and I remember particularly went to Likovac between the Rambouillet and Paris conferences to see the -- what they call themselves General Staff of the KLA. But when -- whether I went through Gornje Obrinje via Likovac, I don't know. But it's nearby and -- but I couldn't tell now which exact road we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the fact that a Red Cross mission came across a mine in Likovac and there were casualties?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There were actually two incidents. One incident was that Canadian KDOM hit a mine, it must have been a bigger mine, a land-mine, and their armoured vehicle was totally destroyed but there were no casualties in this particular instance. And soon thereafter, a car of the ICRC hit a land-mine and at least one local doctor was killed in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who provided first aid immediately after the incident and took the survivors to nearest medical institutions and so on?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I suppose it was the Serbian authorities who got them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, is it something that you know or something that you assume?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And do you know who laid the mine on the road? Who controlled the territory?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Again, I assume. I don't know who laid the mines, but it is -- our assessment was that the KLA laid these mines. And I do know how the Canadians got out. They were lucky enough that their cellphone worked on a nearby hill because their satphone was also destroyed through the -- through hitting the land-mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question pertains to your statement where you say in July 1998 - that's what you said several times - that you went to Malisevo. You accompanied Dr. Albert Rohan, the Secretary-General of the Austrian foreign affairs ministry, and then you mentioned number seven, Mr. Kadri Veseli. And you speak about the so-called Thaqi government, and now I want to know this. I'm not going to go into your notes and dispatches that you sent to your embassy, to Luxembourg, to Vienna, and so on. But I'm going to ask you: What do you consider as your achievement? Do you consider that you actually achieved anything through those contacts with contact number seven and number three, Mr. Veseli and Thaqi respectively. And if yes, what, in your view, was the consequence of the diplomatic efforts pertaining to the contacts with the KLA? Not the politicians but just the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think if there was an achievement it was that they were in the end willing to integrate into a political process, and as it is shown, they have participated in the Rambouillet conference. So I think having contacted them led them into the political process. That's -- that was our aim, and from this perspective we did achieve something through these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And did they cease their operations until the beginning of the NATO air-strikes, the 24th of March, 1999, in other words, and continue their struggle by political means through talks, negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The conflict was, at best, through the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission, detained to a certain degree but it continued. Skirmishes were frequent also thereafter, and I'm talking about the time leading to Rambouillet. Is that what you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was your achievement, your success, that you managed to reach this result that they embarked on political negotiations and that they came up with those platforms. My next question -- I'm not talking about now -- negotiations now. We'll deal with Rambouillet at the end of the cross-examination today. So my next question has to do specifically with the KLA. Are you familiar with all the cease-fire agreements between the Serb security forces and the KLA. That's my first question before the break.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I was not involved in any of these negotiations. I was involved in January 1999 on the exchange of VJ soldiers, but on cease-fire arrangements, no, I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this is time for our break, and I will have no further questions on this because the witness has no knowledge of the cease-fire agreements reached between the KLA and the Serbian security forces. So this is it as far as this topic is concerned. I will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. We've been waiting for a logical moment to interrupt, but we will resume now at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next question. You spoke several times about a diplomat from Great Britain, Mr. David Slinn. Could you please tell us, who was he?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He was at the UK embassy in Belgrade and filled in in the moment Mr. Braithwaite left. He filled in his position and was covering Kosovo from that time on, must have been spring/early summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, to the best of your recollection, what talks did he participate in, who did he talk to while you were both in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He would talk to the same group of people in Pristina, the politicians, and he was not tasked and not given the permission to meet the KLA until end of July shortly before we went together to Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: You mentioned the events in Obrinje, and I have a document here and it's a document D0024615. I think that's the version in B/C/S and the English document is right next to it, so if you could just show the two documents side by side. It's a document from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. We have yet to receive it on our screens. We'll have to wait a while. This is -- okay. Now we have the translation too. A very quick question: Are you familiar with this document from the Ministry of the Interior? It pertains to Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, this is not a document I've seen at the time, but I remember the incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know who Kari Korklo is a forensic pathology expert from Finland, have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He must have been on the team of Finnish pathologists which we had agreed that they would do investigations in three plus three cases, six altogether. But I remember particularly Helena Ranta, she was heading this Finnish team, and Mr. Timo Lahelma who was an ambassador for human rights issues in the Finnish foreign ministry. They both were on this team which -- which was heading out on the 10th of December to Gornje Obrinje to do the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have information that the team of Finnish experts who headed to the site together with the investigating of the Pristina district court, Ms. Danica Marinkovic, actually was not able to reach the site because the site was already under the control of the KLA forces and this created some danger because the investigating judge of that court was escorted by the police? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, I was on this trip. I was in the Austrian car which was at the top of the convoy. There was ECMM, including trucks, and the whole operation was organised before, and it was no problem whatsoever for the Finnish forensic team in -- accompanied by ECMM to go to Gornje Obrinje, as you said, UCK-held territory. It was only this very morning where they headed out to do the actual exhumations, they had prepared the sites beforehand, that not only Mrs. Marinkovic wanted to participate, but as she did not feel safe enough without, we had a long tail of Serbian police cars, armoured vehicles, following our convoy; and we did not enter the UCK-held territory because we knew this would mean a direct clash where we, meaning the Finnish forensic team, ECMM, and myself would have been in the middle. So we did not enter at that particular day and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But it was postponed at the proposal of the investigating judge, Madam Marinkovic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Postponement is a nice word. As it was not possible because the investigating judge insisted to come along with police, these exhumations could not take place. And in the aftermath the Finnish forensic team decided, although everything was prepared, including taking them to Pristina to the forensic laboratory, that they would concentrate on a different site, the one in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00061, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do with the document 2654.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation} It's a 65 ter document, and I would like to ask the usher to show this document in English and in Serbian on our screens -- or in German.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now we have both documents. This document was drafted on the 7th of October, 1998. Did you draft it, and do you recognise this as your document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise my document, and I see that instead of 7 October at the beginning I write 7/9, 7 September, which is a mistake. It was drafted 7 of October and the meeting of Petritsch with Mr. Holbrooke took place on the 7th of October and not the 7th September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will not ask you to quote the UN Security Council Resolution 1199 because we know that, but regarding the comments made in this document could you please explain why this is written in this way and what was the position of the Austrian embassy and what was the position of Mr. Holbrooke regarding this issue or any talks about the actions of the Republic of Serbia and President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, this was the first time that Mr. Holbrooke met with Mr. Petritsch in his capacity as UN Special Envoy on Kosovo. He must have been officially nominated just a few days before. And I remember that I called the US deputy head of mission from Belgrade asking for at least a briefing of Mr. Holbrooke on his talks with Mr. Milosevic because they didn't take us along in these discussions they had with top brass of the leadership -- republic leadership in Belgrade. And he reports, as I cite here, that he had a grim impression that was one of the hardest talks he had with Milosevic in years. Mr. Milosevic told him that all requests of Security Council Resolution 1199 have been fulfilled and that Mr. Holbrooke said that if the talks he held did not have success, were not successful, they would turn an ACTORD. That's I don't know which level of NATO, but this was clearly a threat of bombardment. That's the beginning of October, so that's before what we call the agreement on the Holbrooke package. And about that time, 7 October, I think the early October, the report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 1199 was due.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00062, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 2656 65 ter, both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We have both documents. Mr. Kickert, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is the date on this document correct, the 9th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's the same mistake as before. I wrote it on the 9th of October, and it is on the talk of -- and I was there present of Ambassador Petritsch with Ambassador Kotov on the 9th of October because it makes reference to a meeting on the 8th of October of Mr. Ivanov with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, we have your report here where you say that Russians are still opposed to the use of military force, it's in the second paragraph. And then you go on to say that the Russians believed that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has already put a lot of things in motion in order to fulfil the Security Council Resolution 1999 [as interpreted] requirements. Can you tell me, what was the practical consequence of this discussion between your ambassador and Mr. Kotov and I can see that the Russian Defence Minister Sergeyev is also mentioned here and also Ivanov who he had talks with the then-President of Serbia Milosevic. You say in the end that on the 4th of October Milosevic was pressured to agree to a substantial OSCE mission for Kosovo. So I would like you to comment briefly on the diplomatic talks that you participated in.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That briefing of Russian Ambassador Kotov was to fill Mr. Petritsch in on what the Russians did. As I explained beforehand, there was sort of the US stream, the -- and the Russian stream to -- and I write in my third paragraph that they were trying to convince Mr. Milosevic to agree to international monitors, and the idea was to expand the KDOM into an OSCE mission, like -- as I state in my one, two, three, four, five, sixth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This report of yours obviously confirms what you said a little while ago, that Ambassador Holbrooke threatened air-strikes and any kind of force. What was the Russian position regarding the use of military force? I'm sure that after this discussion you did form some impressions.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I mean, this was not a secret. It was even -- the threat of bombing was even mentioned in public domain, in the media. And this -- whatever these steps were, ACTORD, and so on, these were used as a means to convince - if I may put it that way - the Belgrade leadership to give in and to agree to what then became the OSCE-KVM plus the NATO air surveillance agreement. So there was a whole package which Mr. Holbrooke in the end negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue with another line of questioning I would like to tender this document as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00063, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, since you're a diplomat I'm going to ask you this question. There was mention of threat of military force being used by the most powerful military alliance in the world, NATO, against a sovereign state of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Who was supposed to apply this instrument of pressure or this threat of force against a sovereign country?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: As you're well aware, this is NATO. ACTORD -- is different levels of activating this threat, and all NATO member states would have to agree to this. And I have to add that Austria is not a member of NATO, so I had no insight on what was going on and at which level and -- I don't even know how NATO really works in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question - obviously we did not understand each other very well - is: When we talk about the application of military might of NATO, should have that application of military force been confirmed by a UN resolution because of president? And since you are a career diplomat and an educated man, trained for to be a diplomat, I'm asking you this: Could NATO conduct air-strikes of its own volition, and that would be a unilateral decision of its member states; or could NATO have been able to do so pursuant to a decision of the United Nations? If you can answer, please do so; if not, I'll be content with that as well.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I mean, I would have to look into Security Council Resolution 1199, but I doubt that it was a Chapter 7 resolution which enabled the use of force. I very much doubt that. And the discussion we had after the NATO bombardment, also -- the one which happened and started, as you said, 24 March 1999, was that there was no UN resolution empowering NATO to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude then that this was a decision primarily taken by NATO member states, not all of them but primarily by the United States of America or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: To my knowledge, all NATO member states have to agree to such a decision, but as I said I have no clear insight into the mechanisms -- the decision-making mechanisms of NATO. But as you've seen subsequently in the NATO bombing, that decision was clearly taken by all NATO member states.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is: Do you have any knowledge that NATO had ever before used force against any country anywhere in the world the way that they did then when they conducted air-strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think my recollection that there was bombings in Bosnia, must have been 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Bosnia, you will agree with me that they bombed the position of the Bosnian Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, now I'm sort of just talking what I get from the media. I was never in Bosnia, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. I withdraw my question. My last question or the last topic that we are going to discuss is Rambouillet. What was your role there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: In the moment Mr. Petritsch was named UN Special Envoy I became his assistant because I was dealing with Kosovo, and my particular role was not only to assist him but also to be the liaison with the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that situation did any other diplomats from any other country work with you with respect to Kosovo Albanians or was your role there exclusive to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, no, not exclusive. There was also a German colleague -- because from the beginning of January 1999 Germany took over the EU Presidency and the German colleague was also present and had also contacts with the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was that colleague's name and he acted on behalf of the Federal Republic of Germany or the United Nations or some other country, do you know, and what was his name, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: His name was Axel Dittmann, D-i-t-t-m-a-n-n, and he was a German diplomat, and so representing Germany, but at the same time the EU Presidency in the first half of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge of the time and to the best of your recollection, a mixed composition of the Albanian declaration which included politicians coming from different parts of the spectrums and members of the KLA - I'm not going to name them - did any of them put up anything less in terms of demands other than full independence of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Of course they put up this as their ultimate goal, but the whole Rambouillet accord was not going to be independence. It was going to be -- was about being some sort of autonomy within the -- within the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the basic part of that accord envisaged a final decision on the status of Kosovo being deferred for a number or for a number of years, you can count them on the fingers of one hand, and then to be decided by a referendum of the inhabitants of Kosovo? What would be your answer to this?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was one of the most contentious issues in the Rambouillet accord is what we call the review clause, meaning that at a certain time, in this case I think the last version was three years, there would be a decision on the final status of Kosovo and it avoided the mention of the notion referendum, but it said "taking into account the will of the people."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbian delegation accept such provisions of such an agreement and the eventual, final version that was supposed to be signed in Paris?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, it didn't accept it and they refused in Paris. They said they will not agree to this, the whole agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the Serbian side were told that they were going to be attacked by the mightiest military force in the world had they failed to sign such an agreement?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think it was clear to everybody there that this threat of bombardment was evident. I mean this was clear that should there not be agreement then the bombardment would start, and I think the decision of the Serbian and FRY delegations, they were a mixed composition, was done in the knowledge that this would lead to bombardment. There was after Paris still some last-ditch efforts. The three negotiators Petritsch, Mayorski, and Hill seeing Milosevic and then Holbrooke himself came to Belgrade. And after he left, as we all know, the bombardment started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge about the position of the international community's negotiation team individually, I mean -- by this I mean the leaders of those teams, most important persons, who took part in the negotiations and if you could share this with us, Albright, Holbrooke, Mayorski, Petritsch, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There were three negotiators Chris Hill for the United States, Petritsch for the EU, and then Mayorski for the Russian Federation. Also present in the castle were representatives of the Contact Group and sort of in the large Contact Group also the chairman in office of the OSCE in 1999, that was Norway. So there would be frequent meetings of this Contact Group often with the political directors coming in, and then they were less frequent but also meetings of the Contact Group on ministerial level. We had visits of individual Contact Group ministers. We had the French, we had the British, and we had the US Secretary of State also visiting and staying for quite some days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please relate the positions of the main three figures, the main negotiators, representing the US of A, EU, and Russian Federation after the Serbian side had refused to sign the agreement and when the negotiations fell through.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: You mean now in Paris or at Rambouillet itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In Paris, in Paris, because in Paris we found out that the negotiations fell through and that the bombardment will follow. What was the opinion of the US representative, of Mr. Petritsch, and of Ambassador Mayorski? Was their position unique about the need to bombard the FRY or the Republic of Serbia or not?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, there's also no secret that there were some discrepancies in the opinion, and for sure there was a great degree of disappointment that no decision could be taken in Paris. And I think things have developed so far that nobody could backtrack anymore. As I said, these last-ditch efforts were made in Belgrade where I understood, because I was not present at these meetings, that some offers were made also to Mr. Milosevic maybe to reconsider, to change things. But as we were told there was an outright no, and what happened afterwards was -- is part of history.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, could you please explain your formal academic degrees that you hold. What is your academic education?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I am a geographer and historian by education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now certain things have begun falling into place. Thank you very much and this would be all for me. Thank you for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have finished with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Gopalan, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, I have a few questions about the exhumations in Gornje Obrinje or the attempts as you described it. You mentioned in response to Defence counsel that the original plan -- you mention that the original plan was for the Finnish forensic team and the ECMM to travel to the area and you said that this would not have been a problem. Just to clarify, what was the cause of the problem on that day that resulted in the exhumations not being conducted?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was the that our convoy was accompanied by the Serbian police force because, as I said before, we - and I was even present at least one of the visits to the burial site with the Finnish team - we had access even if it was KLA-controlled, we had full access. And in the terms, in these exchange of letters which I mentioned this morning between the foreign ministers of the FRY and of Finland, there was free access and also -- guaranteed. So we thought that we would do these exhumations. Ms. Marinkovic wanted to be part of it. There was no problem with it. But then when she insisted to take along police, we had to abort this operation or else we would have ended up, as I told before, in between the lines and who knows what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were not able to access the site on that day. Were any steps taken later in the day or in the preceding days to arrange for access to be regained?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, by pure coincidence on this very day the minister of justice was in Pristina, and we were able to secure a meeting with him in the government building in Pristina, and we complained about what had happened. He was not in a position to grant us what we wanted, meaning access on our own to do the exhumations and bring the people -- the exhumed people to Pristina on our own. It was later then also in the month brought up in Belgrade by Ambassador Petritsch but to no avail. The Finnish team then packed their things and went for Christmas holidays.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You also said that following access being denied to this site, specific site, Gornje Obrinje, the Finns decided to concentrate on Orahovac. Did they face any access issues in that site?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, that was -- Orahovac was controlled by Serbian police, so there was no access whatsoever -- no access problem, sorry, no access problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you give us a little bit of background as to what incident was being investigated in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was this allegation of mass graves in a waste dump. So the idea was to exhume the bodies there as well and try to - I'm not a forensic expert - to get some information on who these people were and how they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And just my final question going back to Gornje Obrinje: Do you know if exhumations were conducted there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Maybe after the NATO bombing. I'm not aware that there were done beforehand, because then things were overtaken by events because then we -- we entered the phase of Racak and so the -- on the -- the whole concentration of the international community was then on this particular incident and no longer on the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So just to clarify, prior to the NATO bombing, to your knowledge there were no exhumations that were conducted in Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no. But from beginning of 1999 I was no longer directly responsible for -- for the Finnish team because they worked for the EU, and then my German colleagues would take over dealing with them directly and no longer myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Kickert. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, you'll be pleased to know that once again we have come to the end of the questions for you. We would thank you for your attendance here and the assistance you've been able to give, and you of course may now return to your normal activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and thank you also the Prosecution and the Defence that I could finish today. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we've got two minutes to go. I don't think there's any point in trying to occupy that. We shall adjourn for the day and resume Monday afternoon, at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of March, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
